{{short description|Statistical tool}}
{{context|date=December 2015}}

In linear [[panel analysis]], it can be desirable to estimate the magnitude of the [[fixed effects]], as they provide measures of the [[latent variable|unobserved components]]. For instance, in [[wage equation]] regressions, fixed effects capture [[Latent and observable variables|unobservable]]s that are constant over time, such as motivation. [[Gary Chamberlain|Chamberlain]]'s approach to unobserved effects models is a way of estimating the linear unobserved effects, under fixed effect (rather than [[random effects]]) assumptions, in the following unobserved effects model

:<math>y_{it} = x_{it} b + c_i + u_{it}</math>

where ''c<sub>i</sub>'' is the unobserved effect and ''x<sub>it</sub>'' contains only time-varying [[explanatory variables]].<ref name="Wooldridge2002">Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass.</ref>  Rather than [[first-difference estimator|differencing out]] the unobserved effect ''c<sub>i</sub>'', Chamberlain proposed to replace it with the [[linear projection]] of it onto the explanatory variables in all time periods. Specifically, this leads to the following equation

:<math>c_i = d + x_{i1} \lambda_1 + x_{i2} \lambda_2 + \dots + x_{iT} \lambda_T + e_i</math>

where the [[Conditional probability distribution|conditional distribution]] of ''c<sub>i</sub>''  given ''x<sub>it</sub>'' is unspecified, as is standard in fixed effects models. Combining these equations then gives rise to the following model.<ref>Chamberlain, G. (1982): Multivariate Regression Models for Panel Data. Journal of Econometrics (18), pp. 5-46</ref><ref>Chamberlain, G. (1984): Panel Data. Handbook of Econometrics, Volume 2, ed. Z. Griliches and M. D. Intriligator. Amsterdam: North Holland, pp. 1247-1318</ref>

:<math>y_{it} = d + x_{i1} \lambda_1 + \dots + x_{it} (b + \lambda_t) + \dots + x_{iT} \lambda_T + e_i + u_{it}</math>

An important advantage of this approach is the computational requirement. Chamberlain uses [[minimum distance estimation]], but a [[generalized method of moments]] approach would be another valid way of estimating this model. The latter approach also gives rise to a larger number of [[Instrumental variable|instruments]] than moment conditions, which leads to useful [[overidentifying restrictions]] that can be used to test the [[strict exogeneity restrictions]] imposed by many static Fixed Effects models.<ref name="Wooldridge2002"/>

Similar approaches have been proposed to model the unobserved effect. For instance, Mundlak follows a very similar approach, but rather projects the unobserved effect ''c<sub>i</sub>'' onto the average of all ''x<sub>it</sub>'' across all ''T'' time periods, more specifically <ref>Mundlak, Y. (1978): On the Pooling of Time Series and Cross Section Data. Econometrica (46), pp. 69-85</ref>

:<math>c_i = d + \overline{x}_i \lambda + e_i</math>

It can be shown that the Chamberlain method is a generalization of Mundlak's model. The Chamberlain method has been popular in [[applied economics|empirical work]], ranging from studies trying to estimate the causal returns to [[Trade union|union]] membership,<ref>Card, D. (1996): The effect of unions on the structure of wages: a longitudinal analysis. Econometrica (64), pp. 957-979</ref> to studies investigating [[growth convergence]],<ref>Islam, N. (1995): Growth Empirics: A Panel Data Approach. The Quarterly Journal of Economics (110), pp. 1127-1170</ref> and estimating product characteristics in [[Supply and demand|demand estimation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nevo|first=Aviv|date=March 2001|title=Measuring Market Power in the Ready-to-Eat Cereal Industry |journal=Econometrica|volume=69|issue=2|pages=307–342|doi=10.1111/1468-0262.00194|s2cid=9708178 |issn=0012-9682}}</ref>
